name: Dakota
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: (d) Dakota (Siouan, Great Plains; Chambers 1978; Shaw 1985a, 1985b). Stress falls on the second syllable of a word, and on monosyllables. This suggests that a single even iamb is assigned at the left edge of a word.

new_statements.quote: Most surface forms in Dakota are characterized by stress on the second syllable from the left edge of the word, as illustrated in (1) (unless otherwise indicated, the data are from Shaw 1976 and 1985). (1) čhikté 'I kill you'; wičháyakte 'you kill them'; owį́čhayaktepiktešni 'you will not kill them there'. Shaw (1985) analyzes this pattern as the building of a noniterative iambic foot at the left edge of the word, however, both Shaw (1985) and Sietsema (1988) claim that syllable weight plays no role in determining stress in Dakota. [p. 47] ... Bisyllabic surface forms analyzed in Chambers 1974, Shaw 1976, and Sietsema 1988 as underlyingly CVC bear initial stress. [p. 49]

The only difference from the compiler quote is the extracted text rendering of the nasal hook + acute on the third e…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2 second stress = second syllable from the left): 'stress on the second syllable from the left edge of the word'. Adds: weight plays no role (Shaw 1985, Sietsema 1988), the foot is noniterative (single stress per word), and three exception classes with initial stress: underlying CVC roots with epenthetic final [a] (čhápa 'beaver', šúka 'dog', čéka 'to stagger'), monosyllabic stems plus unstressable postnominal/postverbal clitics (mníkį 'the water', špą́šni 'it's not cooked'), and syntactic compounds, which carry one stress on each constituent (hą́wakhą́ 'holy night' vs lexical compound hąwákhą 'northern lights'). Data are attributed to Shaw 197…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the second syllable of the word counting from the left, regardless of syllable weight, one stress per word (noniterative). Initial stress instead in three classes: bisyllabic words that are underlyingly CVC roots with an epenthetic final -a; monosyllabic stems followed by (always unstressed) clitics; and the constituents of syntactic (compositional) compounds, each of which keeps its own stress, so a monosyllabic first member is stressed on its first syllable. Lexical (opaque) compounds take the regular second-syllable stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No rhythmic secondary stress: the analysis is explicitly noniterative (ranking ALIGN over PARSE, p. 48). Syntactic compounds carry two stresses, one per constituent (e.g. mníwaxcàxca 'water flower' p. 50), which is the only source of a second prominence in a word.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) CVC roots: čhápa 'beaver', šúka 'dog', čéka 'to stagger' bear initial stress (p. 49); (ii) postnominal/postverbal clitics never receive stress (Shaw 1976:39), so monosyllable + clitic surfaces with initial stress: mníkį 'the water', špą́šni 'it's not cooked', čhíkešni (p. 49); (iii) syntactic compounds bear two stresses, one on each constituent, hą́wakhą́ 'holy night', while lexical compounds have regular second-syllable stress, hąwákhą 'northern lights' (p. 50). Suffixal reduplication and -ya suffixation on monosyllabic roots keep regular second-syllable stress: čekčéka, saksáka, ptus-yá, ska-yá (pp. 49-50).
new_statements.identity_note: Kennedy 1994 does not name a dialect; his footnote 1 describes Dakota as 'a member of the Mississippian Valley subfamily of Siouan.. spoken in the Northern Great Plains area of the United States and Canada', and his data are taken from Shaw 1976 and 1985. Simons 2024 is explicitly a grammar of the Santee-Sisseton dialect (title), but it was not opened. Glottolog codes Simons's language as 'Santee-Sisseton = Dakota [dak]'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the verified primary quotation (Riggs 1893:5 §4.2) and the database quotation (Hayes 1995:267 + fn.19) are present verbatim in copies we hold at the stated places. (2) Source quality: the peninitial rule is multiply and consistently attested — Riggs 1893 (Santee, primary), Boas & Deloria 1941 §23 (Teton), Shaw 1985a:175 via StressTyp2, Hayes 1995:267, Kennedy 1994:47 — so the rule string 01/010/0100.. is secure and dialect-appropriate.
